parts.label: (a)
parts.part_stem: A sphere in a liquid accelerates vertically downwards from rest. For the viscous force acting on the moving sphere, state:

parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a viscous force tries to do to motion through a liquid - does it help the sphere fall faster or hold it back?
parts.proper_answer: Vertically upwards, opposite to the downward motion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Drag As Opposition**
Imagine pushing your hand through water. You feel the water pushing back against your movement. Viscous force, also called drag, always acts to oppose the velocity of the object relative to the fluid.

Step 2: **Apply To Falling Sphere**
Here the sphere moves vertically downwards, so the liquid must push back vertically upwards. That is the direction of the viscous force.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: the variation, if any, in the magnitude.
hints: Hint 1: The sphere starts from rest and speeds up downwards - think about how the strength of drag is linked to how fast the object is moving.
parts.proper_answer: Increases as the speed (velocity) of the sphere increases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Drag To Speed**
For a small sphere moving in a fluid, faster motion means more fluid has to be pushed aside each second, so the resistive viscous force gets larger. In simple terms, drag grows when speed grows.

Step 2: **Follow The Motion**
The sphere accelerates downwards from rest, so its downward speed keeps increasing at first. Therefore the upward viscous force acting on it must also increase in magnitude.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A man of weight $750\text{ N}$ stands a distance of $3.6\text{ m}$ from end D of a horizontal uniform beam AD, as shown in Fig. 4.1.
{{figure:figure_4_1}}
Fig. 4.1 (not to scale)
The beam has a weight of $380\text{ N}$ and a length of $9.0\text{ m}$. The beam is supported by a vertical force $F_{\text{B}}$ at pivot B and a vertical force $F_{\text{C}}$ at pivot C. Pivot B is a distance of $2.0\text{ m}$ from end A and pivot C is a distance of $2.0\text{ m}$ from end D. The beam is in equilibrium.

parts.label: (b)(i)

markscheme_points.text: sum/total of clockwise moments about a point = sum/total of anticlockwise moments about the (same) point

hints: Hint 1: Remember that a balanced beam does not start to rotate - think about what that means for the turning effects trying to spin it one way versus the other way.
Hint 2: Focus on making the statement complete: the two total turning effects must be equal, and they must be calculated about the same point or pivot.
parts.proper_answer: For a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What No Rotation Means**
A moment is force times perpendicular distance from a pivot, $moment = F \times d$. It tells you how strongly a force tries to turn something. If the beam stays level and balanced, the total tendency to turn clockwise must exactly cancel the total tendency to turn anticlockwise.

Step 2: **Full Precise Statement**
So for rotational equilibrium: $$ \sum M_{clockwise} = \sum M_{anticlockwise} $$ where all moments are taken about the same point. Missing the idea of equilibrium or the same point loses marks, so include both.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: By using moments about pivot C, calculate $F_{\text{B}}$.
hints: Hint 1: Taking moments about C removes $F_C$ from the equation - work out the three perpendicular distances from C: to B, to the beam centre, and to the man.
Hint 2: Set the anticlockwise moment from $F_B$ equal to the sum of the clockwise moments from the two weights, then rearrange to find $F_B$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find All Distances From C**
You are beside the diagram, so measure everything from pivot C. The beam is $9.0\text{ m}$ long, B is $2.0\text{ m}$ from A and C is $2.0\text{ m}$ from D, so $$ BC = 9.0 - 2.0 - 2.0 = 5.0\text{ m} $$ The uniform $380\text{ N}$ weight acts at the middle, $4.5\text{ m}$ from A. C is $7.0\text{ m}$ from A, so the weight is $$ 7.0 - 4.5 = 2.5\text{ m} $$ to the left of C. The $750\text{ N}$ man is $3.6\text{ m}$ from D while C is $2.0\text{ m}$ from D, so the man is $$ 3.6 - 2.0 = 1.6\text{ m} $$ to the left of C.

Step 2: **Balance Moments About C**
$F_B$ pulls up $5.0\text{ m}$ left of C, giving an anticlockwise moment. Both weights pull down left of C, giving clockwise moments. For equilibrium: $$ F_B \times 5.0 = 380 \times 2.5 + 750 \times 1.6 $$ $$ F_B \times 5.0 = 950 + 1200 = 2150 $$ $$ F_B = \frac{2150}{5.0} = 430\text{ N} $$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The man walks towards end D. The beam is about to tip when $F_{\text{B}}$ becomes zero.
Determine the minimum distance $x$ from end D that the man can stand without tipping the beam.

markscheme_points.text:
moments may be taken about other points, e.g. about D:
(380 × 4.5) + (750 × x) = 1130 × 2.0

hints: Hint 1: When the beam is just about to tip over C, contact at B is lost so $F_B = 0$ - think about which pivot the beam will now rotate around and take moments there.
Hint 2: Let the man be distance $x$ from D, so his distance from C is $(2.0 - x)$ - equate the clockwise moment of the man to the anticlockwise moment of the beam weight.
parts.proper_answer: Moments about C with $F_B = 0$: $380 \times 2.5 = 750 \times (2.0 - x)$, giving $x = 0.73\text{ m} \approx 0.7\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Understand The Tipping Point**
As the man walks toward D he moves to the right of C and his weight starts to tip the beam clockwise over C. The left support at B pushes up less and less. Just as the beam lifts off B, $F_B = 0$ and C becomes the only pivot. That is the limiting balance.

Step 2: **Balance Moments About C**
The $380\text{ N}$ beam weight is still $2.5\text{ m}$ left of C, holding the beam down on the left. The man is now $x$ from D, and C is $2.0\text{ m}$ from D, so the man is $(2.0 - x)$ to the right of C. Equate moments: $$ 380 \times 2.5 = 750 \times (2.0 - x) $$ $$ 950 = 750 \times (2.0 - x) $$ $$ 2.0 - x = \frac{950}{750} = 1.27\text{ m} $$ $$ x = 2.0 - 1.27 = 0.73\text{ m} \approx 0.7\text{ m} $$ This is the closest he can get to D; any smaller $x$ tips the beam.
